newsitem.title: JAPAN: Hanwa Bank had a troubled past.
newsitem.headline: Hanwa Bank had a troubled past.

text.p: Established in 1941 in western Japan, Hanwa Bank became a classic victim of the bubble economy of the 1980s and its own mismanagement.
Its main business territory was in the rougher confines of Osaka and Wakayama, far from the blue-chip banking dynasties of Japan.
It even had a top executive responsible for problem loans gunned down outside his home.

The company hit its high-water mark in the late 1980s. Its profits peaked at 3.66 billion yen ($32.9 million) in the fiscal year ending March 1988 and it went public on the Osaka Securities Exchange the following year.
But loans to finance grandiose real estate schemes caught up with it.
In August 1993 Tomosaburo Koyama, a vice president in charge of recovering bad loans from a related company, was shot dead in front of his home.
Its offices became a virtual revolving door of newly appointed presidents who were brought in but failed to clean up the mess.
The latest chief executive, former Ministry of Finance official Takeshi Shinkyo, presented his resignation hours after the closure was announced.
Its financial problems were long-rumoured and long-denied.
In April it said that it was not in financial difficulty and just two weeks ago said it would have a moderate loss of 280 million yen ($2.52 million) for the six months ending September 30.

But its last forecast was no better than the bad loans it gave out over the past 10 years. When the figures were announced on Thursday, the actual loss was 120 times higher at 33.72 billion yen ($303 million). ($1=111 yen)
